entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16029"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 18</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Acts.18.1-Acts.18.22">Ac 18:1-22</reference>. Paul's Arrival and Labors at Corinth, Where He Is Rejoined by Silas and Timothy, and, under Divine Encouragement, Makes a Long Stay--At Length, Retracing His Steps, by Ephesus, Cæsarea, and Jerusalem, He Returns for the Last Time to Antioch, Thus Completing His Second Missionary Journey.</title> <div sID="gen30953" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16029"/><hi type="bold">1-4. came to Corinth--</hi>rebuilt by Julius Cæsar on the isthmus between the Ægean and Ionian Seas; the capital of the Roman province of Achaia, and the residence of the proconsul; a large and populous mercantile city, and the center of commerce alike for East and West; having a considerable Jewish population, larger, probably, at this time than usual, owing to the banishment of the Jews from Rome by Claudius Cæsar (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.2">Ac 18:2</reference>). Such a city was a noble field for the Gospel, which, once established there, would naturally diffuse itself far and wide. <div eID="gen30953" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16033"/><div sID="gen30959" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16033"/><hi type="bold">5-6. And when Silas and Timotheus were come from Macedonia--</hi>that is, from Thessalonica, whither Silas had probably accompanied Timothy when sent back from Athens (see on <reference osisRef="Acts.17.15">Ac 17:15</reference>).<div eID="gen30959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30960" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Paul was pressed in the spirit--</hi>rather (according to what is certainly the true reading) "was pressed with the word"; expressing not only his zeal and assiduity in preaching it, but some inward pressure which at this time he experienced in the work (to convey which more clearly was probably the origin of the common reading). What that pressure was we happen to know, with singular minuteness and vividness of description, from the apostle himself, in his first Epistles to the Corinthians and Thessalonians (<reference osisRef="1Cor.2.1-1Cor.2.5">1Co 2:1-5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.3.1-1Thess.3.10">1Th 3:1-10</reference>). He had come away from Athens, as he remained there, in a depressed and anxious state of mind, having there met, for the first time, with unwilling Gentile ears. He continued, apparently for some time, laboring alone in the synagogue of Corinth, full of deep and anxious solicitude for his Thessalonian converts. His early ministry at Corinth was colored by these feelings. Himself deeply humbled, his power as a preacher was more than ever felt to lie in demonstration of the Spirit. At length Silas and Timotheus arrived with exhilarating tidings of the faith and love of his Thessalonian children, and of their earnest longing again to see their father in Christ; bringing with them also, in token of their love and duty, a pecuniary contribution for the supply of his wants. This seems to have so lifted him as to put new life and vigor into his ministry. He now wrote his First Epistle to the Thessalonians, in which the "pressure" which resulted from all this strikingly appears. (See Introduction to First Thessalonians). Such emotions are known only to the ministers of Christ, and, even of them, only to such as "travail in birth until Christ be formed in" their hearers. <div eID="gen30960" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16035"/><div sID="gen30963" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16035"/><hi type="bold">7-8. he departed thence, and entered into a certain man's house, named Justus--</hi>not changing his lodging, as if Aquila and Priscilla up to this time were with the opponents of the apostle [Alford], but merely ceasing any more to testify in the synagogue, and henceforth carrying on his labors in this house of Justus, which "joining hard to the synagogue," would be easily accessible to such of its worshippers as were still open to light. Justus, too, being probably a proselyte, would more easily draw a mixed audience than the synagogue. From this time forth conversions rapidly increased. <div eID="gen30963" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16046"/><div sID="gen30979" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16046"/><hi type="bold">18. Paul ... tarried ... yet a good while--</hi>During his long residence at Corinth, Paul planted other churches in Achaia (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.1">2Co 1:1</reference>).<div eID="gen30979" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30980" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then took ... leave of the brethren, and sailed ... into--</hi>rather, "for"<div eID="gen30980" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30981" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Syria--</hi>to Antioch, the starting-point of all the missions to the Gentiles, which he feels to be for the present concluded.<div eID="gen30981" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30982" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with him Priscilla and Aquila--</hi>In this order the names also occur in <reference osisRef="Acts.18.26">Ac 18:26</reference> (according to the true reading); compare <reference osisRef="Rom.16.3">Ro 16:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.19">2Ti 4:19</reference>, which seem to imply that the wife was the more prominent and helpful to the Church. Silas and Timotheus doubtless accompanied the apostle, as also Erastus, Gaius, and Aristarchus (<reference osisRef="Acts.19.22">Ac 19:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.19.29">29</reference>). Of Silas, as Paul's associate, we read no more. His name occurs last in connection with Peter and the churches of Asia Minor [Webster and Wilkinson].<div eID="gen30982" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30983" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having shorn his head in Cenchrea--</hi>the eastern harbor of Corinth, about ten miles distant, where a church had been formed (<reference osisRef="Rom.16.1">Ro 16:1</reference>).<div eID="gen30983" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30984" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for he--</hi>Paul.<div eID="gen30984" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30985" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">had a vow--</hi>That it was the Nazarite vow (<reference osisRef="Num.6.1-Num.6.27">Nu 6:1-27</reference>) is not likely. It was probably one made in one of his seasons of difficulty or danger, in prosecution of which he cuts off his hair and hastens to Jerusalem to offer the requisite sacrifice within the prescribed thirty days [Josephus, Wars of the Jews, 2.15.1]. This explains the haste with which he leaves Ephesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.21">Ac 18:21</reference>), and the subsequent observance, on the recommendation of the brethren, of a similar vow (<reference osisRef="Acts.21.24">Ac 21:24</reference>). This one at Corinth was voluntary, and shows that even in heathen countries he systematically studied the prejudices of his Jewish brethren. <div eID="gen30985" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 18. Paul ... tarried ... yet a good while-- During his long residence at Corinth, Paul planted other churches in Achaia ( 2Co 1:1 ). then took ... leave of the brethren, and sailed ... into-- rather, "for" Syria-- to Antioch, the starting-point of all the missions to the Gentiles, which he feels to be for the present concluded. with him Priscilla and Aquila-- In this order the names also occur in Ac 18:26 (according to the true reading); compare Ro 16:3 ; 2Ti 4:19 , which seem to imply that the wife was the more prominent and helpful to the Church. Silas and Timotheus doubtless accompanied the apostle, as also Erastus, Gaius, and Aristarchus ( Ac 19:22 , 29 ). Of Silas, as Paul's associate, we read no more. His name occurs last in connection with Peter and the churches of Asia Minor [Webster and Wilkinson]. having shorn his head in Cenchrea-- the eastern harbor of Corinth, about ten miles distant, where a church had been formed ( Ro 16:1 ). for he-- Paul. had a vow-- That it was the Nazarite vow ( Nu 6:1-27 ) is not likely. It was probably one made in one of his seasons of difficulty or danger, in prosecution of which he cuts off his hair and hastens to Jerusalem to offer the requisite sacrifice within the prescribed thirty days [Josephus, Wars of the Jews, 2.15.1]. This explains the haste with which he leaves Ephesus ( Ac 18:21 ), and the subsequent observance, on the recommendation of the brethren, of a similar vow ( Ac 21:24 ). This one at Corinth was voluntary, and shows that even in heathen countries he systematically studied the prejudices of his Jewish brethren.

It was a sail, right across from the west to the east side of the Ægean Sea, of some eight or ten days, with a fair wind.<div eID="gen30986" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30987" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">left them there--</hi>Aquila and Priscilla.<div eID="gen30987" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30988" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but he himself entered into the synagogue--</hi>merely taking advantage of the vessel putting in there.<div eID="gen30988" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30989" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and reasoned with the Jews--</hi>the tense here not being the usual one denoting continuous action (as in <reference osisRef="Acts.17.2">Ac 17:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.18.4">18:4</reference>), but that expressing a transient act. He had been forbidden to preach the word in Asia (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.6">Ac 16:6</reference>), but he would not consider that as precluding this passing exercise of his ministry when Providence brought him to its capital; nor did it follow that the prohibition was still in force. <div eID="gen30989" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 19. he came to Ephesus-- the capital of the Roman province of Asia. (See Introduction to Ephesians). It was a sail, right across from the west to the east side of the Ægean Sea, of some eight or ten days, with a fair wind. left them there-- Aquila and Priscilla. but he himself entered into the synagogue-- merely taking advantage of the vessel putting in there. and reasoned with the Jews-- the tense here not being the usual one denoting continuous action (as in Ac 17:2 ; 18:4 ), but that expressing a transient act. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16050"/><div sID="gen30993" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16050"/><hi type="bold">22. And when he had landed at Cæsarea--</hi>where he left the vessel.<div eID="gen30993" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30994" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and gone up--</hi>that is, to Jerusalem.<div eID="gen30994" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30995" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and saluted the church--</hi>In these few words does the historian despatch the apostle's FOURTH VISIT TO Jerusalem after his conversion. The expression "going up" is invariably used of a journey to the metropolis; and thence he naturally "went down to Antioch." Perhaps the vessel reached too late for the feast, as he seems to have done nothing in Jerusalem beyond "saluting the Church," and privately offering the sacrifice with which his vow (<reference osisRef="Acts.18.18">Ac 18:18</reference>) would conclude. It is left to be understood, as on his arrival from his first missionary tour, that "when he was come, and had gathered the church together, he rehearsed all that God had done with him" (<reference osisRef="Acts.14.27">Ac 14:27</reference>) on this his second missionary journey.<div eID="gen30995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30996" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Ac 18:23-21:16. Paul's Third and Last Missionary Journey--</hi>He Visits the Churches of Galatia and Phrygia. <div eID="gen30996" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv16051"/><div sID="gen30997" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv16051"/><hi type="bold">23. And after he had spent some time there--</hi>but probably not long.<div eID="gen30997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30998" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he departed--</hi>little thinking, probably, he was never more to return to Antioch.<div eID="gen30998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen30999" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went over all ... Galatia and Phrygia in order--</hi>visiting the several churches in succession. See on <reference osisRef="Acts.16.6">Ac 16:6</reference>. Galatia is mentioned first here, as he would come to it first from Antioch. It was on this visitation that he ordained the weekly collection (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.1">1Co 16:1</reference>, 2), which has been since adopted generally, and converted into a public usage throughout Christendom. (In what appears to be the true reading of this verse, Priscilla is put before Aquila, as in <reference osisRef="Acts.18.18">Ac 18:18</reference> [see on Ac 18:18]; she being probably the more intelligent and devoted of the two). One cannot but observe how providential it was that this couple should have been left at Ephesus when Paul sailed thence for Syria; and no doubt it was chiefly to pave the way for the better understanding of this episode that the fact is expressly mentioned by the historian in <reference osisRef="Acts.18.19">Ac 18:19</reference>. We see here also an example of not only lay agency (as it is called), but female agency of the highest kind and with the most admirable fruit. Nor can one help admiring the humility and teachableness of so gifted a teacher in sitting at the feet of a Christian woman and her husband. <div eID="gen31011" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_plain: 27-28. And when he was disposed-- "minded," "resolved." to pass into Achaia-- of which Corinth, on the opposite coast (see on Ac 18:1 ), was the capital; there to proclaim that Gospel which he now more fully comprehended. the brethren-- We had not before heard of such gathered at Ephesus. But the desire of the Jews to whom Paul preached to retain him among them for some time ( Ac 18:20 ), and his promise to return to them ( Ac 18:21 ), seem to indicate some drawing towards the Gospel, which, no doubt, the zealous private labors of Priscilla and Aquila would ripen into discipleship. wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him-- a beautiful specimen of "letters of recommendation" (as Ac 15:23 , 25-27 , and see 2Co 3:1 ); by which, as well as by interchange of deputations, &c., the early churches maintained active Christian fellowship with each other. when he was come, helped them much-- was a great acquisition to the Achaian brethren. which believed through grace-- one of those incidental expressions which show that faith's being a production of God's grace in the heart was so current and recognized a truth that it was taken for granted, as a necessary consequence of the general system of grace, rather than expressly insisted on. (It is against the natural order of the words to read them, as Bengel, Meyer, and others, do, "helped through grace those who believed").
